✦ Sourcing focuses on supplier selection.

Simply put:
Procurement = Sourcing + Purchasing ➝ combined to support sustainable and cost-effective operations.

Industrial Engineers have always helped organizations answer:
“How do we make systems safer, faster, and more efficient?”

As AI becomes embedded into these systems, a new question emerges:
“How do we make AI trustworthy?”

This is where Industrial Engineers have an opportunity to contribute.

Many of the skills we already use are becoming essential for responsible AI implementation:
✓ Risk assessment
✓ Process controls
✓ Failure Mode & Effects Analysis (FMEA)
✓ Validation and documentation
✓ Continuous improvement
✓ Human-centered system design

The EU AI Act reflects a shift toward a risk-based approach to AI, asking organizations to move beyond:

“Can we build it?”
and start asking:
→ Is it safe?
→ Is it transparent?
→ Can we monitor it?
→ Can humans remain accountable?

While the EU AI Act is European regulation, its impact extends beyond Europe.
Whether you are in the US, Philippines, Europe, or anywhere else, if you work with AI-enabled products, automation, analytics, or operational systems, these conversations will eventually reach your organization.

AI governance is becoming the next evolution of systems engineering.
Industrial Engineers have always improved the way systems work.
Now, we have the opportunity to help shape how intelligent systems work.

AI will never do a gemba walk.

It can't feel the vibration of a struggling machine. 
It can't see the workaround your operator quietly built last Tuesday. 
It can't smell the difference between normal and abnormal.

And yet, AI is being used for decisions it was never designed to make. Not out of negligence, because the governance framework doesn't exist yet.

That gap is expensive.

I'm currently researching AI governance in operational excellence, still a sensitive and evolving topic, so I'll keep my findings close for now. If you want to go deeper on what I'm exploring, I write about it on Substack → https://lnkd.in/g8kMjf4c

AI is your staff engineer. Not your floor engineer.
Use it for what it's brilliant at, calculating, drafting, structuring, synthesizing data at speed.

But the moment a decision requires physical presence, tacit knowledge, or safety sign-off — you go first. AI follows. The decision table above tells you exactly where that line is. 

────୨ৎ────
What is AI governance for IEs? → https://lnkd.in/gtrUFngB
────୨ৎ────

The 4 starter prompts show you how to use AI after you've done the floor work.
📋 Full prompts suscribe here → https://lnkd.in/g8kMjf4c

AI audit check — before any deliverable "Review this [analysis/SOP/FMEA]. Flag any assumption that requires physical observation or gemba to verify. List them."
Data confidence — before feeding numbers in "I have [X] weeks of cycle time data from [process]. What decisions can I safely make from this, and what needs direct observation?"
Gemba prep — AI makes your walk smarter "I'm doing a gemba walk on [process]. Based on this data, what 5 things should I specifically look for on the floor?"
Risk gate — before safety outputs "Draft an FMEA for [process]. Mark every severity ≥7 row with ⚠️ — these need engineer sign-off, not AI output."

────୨ৎ────
Save this. Send it to your team. 
This is the framework I use before every AI-assisted deliverable.

⚠️ Never input sensitive or proprietary data into external AI tools. Use anonymized or simulated data for learning and testing. 
⚠️ Follow your company's AI usage policies before implementing any workflow. ⚠️ These prompts are guides, not substitutes for professional engineering judgment.

€35 million.
Or 7% of your global revenue. Whichever is bigger.
That's what the EU AI Act can cost you - and it's not a future problem. Parts of it are already law:
→ "Unacceptable risk" AI: banned since Feb 2025
→ General-purpose AI rules: in force since Aug 2025
→ Transparency duties: live August 2, 2026
The Act sorts every AI system into four tiers - from "just add a disclosure" to "banned outright." Where yours land decides whether compliance is a checkbox or a rebuild.
Most leaders assume they're in the safe tier. Most are wrong.
Hiring tools. Credit scoring. Anything touching someone's livelihood → high-risk.
Good news: the EU just extended the heaviest high-risk obligations to December 2027.
 Bad news: the clock on everything else is already running.
Which tier is your AI actually in?

items.content:
I was on a flight when an ad for Industrial AI played on the seatback screen.
And my first thought was... they got the audience right.

I've worked in tech. I've worked in aviation. I know who flies long-haul on a weekday.

But my second thought stuck with me longer.

*Gilbreth had a stopwatch and a camera. 

She wasn't trying to replace workers, she was trying to understand how they moved, where they got tired, what the system was actually costing people. The tool was never the point. The thinking was.

AI is a much faster stopwatch. But it doesn't know why the motion matters.
That part, the curiosity, the ethics, the "go see for yourself"... that's not an inefficiency to automate. That's what industrial engineering actually is.

I worry a little about IE students today. Not because AI will take their jobs. But because if they let AI do the double-checking, they might forget why double-checking mattered in the first place.

The rigor isn't the tedious part. The rigor is the job.

Wrote a deeper piece on this, especially the part about why “rigor” might become the most valuable skill in the AI era. 

Link in comments. 🔗 

*Frank and Lillian Gilbreth: Known for their pioneering work in motion studies and human factors (ergonomics), they are also considered key figures in the development of industrial engineering.

The gemba walk was perfect.
The documentation was the waste.

But it's not just VSMs.

It's the A3 you're writing from scratch for the third time this month.
The 5-why that takes half a day to format.
The SOP nobody updates because it takes too long.
The FMEA you rebuild every time a new line starts up.

All of it. Starting from a blank page. Every single time.

So I set up Claude as my CI agent, ONCE.

My site. My metrics. My waste types. My process language.

Now I walk the floor, come back, and the framework is already waiting.
I just fill in what I observed.

The 3-step setup is in the infographic below. ↓

To the engineers who say AI can't replace a gemba walk, you're right.
It was never supposed to.

The question is: what are you doing with the hours you save after?

And if you're a fresh grad trying to figure out how to compete in this job market, this setup is your head start. You don't need 10 years on the floor to deliver real CI work. You need the right tools, the right methodology, and a senior who's willing to show you the ropes. Start here.

💡 Pro tip: Don't do this alone. Find a senior IE or Black Belt and trade knowledge, they bring the floor experience and the war stories, you bring the AI fluency. That combination is unbeatable. Reach out to your seniors. Learn from their experience. And teach them what you've learned about Claude too.

That's how we all move forward together.

I was on a flight when an ad for Industrial AI played on the seatback screen.
And my first thought was... they got the audience right.

I've worked in tech. I've worked in aviation. I know who flies long-haul on a weekday.

But my second thought stuck with me longer.

*Gilbreth had a stopwatch and a camera. 

She wasn't trying to replace workers, she was trying to understand how they moved, where they got tired, what the system was actually costing people. The tool was never the point. The thinking was.

AI is a much faster stopwatch. But it doesn't know why the motion matters.
That part, the curiosity, the ethics, the "go see for yourself"... that's not an inefficiency to automate. That's what industrial engineering actually is.

I worry a little about IE students today. Not because AI will take their jobs. But because if they let AI do the double-checking, they might forget why double-checking mattered in the first place.

The rigor isn't the tedious part. The rigor is the job.

Wrote a deeper piece on this, especially the part about why “rigor” might become the most valuable skill in the AI era. 

Link in comments. 🔗 

*Frank and Lillian Gilbreth: Known for their pioneering work in motion studies and human factors (ergonomics), they are also considered key figures in the development of industrial engineering.

Nobody’s talking about how AI Ops is basically Industrial Engineering (IE) rebranded for the software era. 

IE has always been about eliminating waste, redesigning workflows, and optimizing systems, not just adding tools on top of broken processes.

That’s exactly what Dr. Ayesha Khanna is describing. Companies are bolting AI onto legacy processes and wondering why nothing improves. IEs have known this for decades: you fix the process first, then you apply the technology.

The “AI workflows” role she mentions? IEs are already trained for this:

	•	Value Stream Mapping to identify where AI can eliminate bottlenecks and reduce lead time
	•	Elimination of Non-Value-Adding Activities (NVA) muda, mura, and muri, before automating waste into the system
	•	Process Mapping & Redesign to determine what gets fully automated, what stays AI-assisted, and what requires human judgment
	•	Time & Motion Studies reimagined, analyzing digital workflows for cycle time reduction
	•	Continuous Improvement (Kaizen) loops to iterate and refine AI-assisted processes
	•	KPI dashboards & OEE thinking applied to knowledge work, not just the shop floor
	•	DMAIC methodology to define, measure, and control AI workflow performance

The real opportunity for IEs right now is to bridge the gap, bring domain process knowledge that pure AI-native grads don’t have yet, and pair it with AI fluency.

That’s not a threat to the profession. That’s a massive expansion of scope.

The companies stuck in “AI pilot purgatory” don’t need more data scientists. They need systems thinkers.

That’s #IndustrialEngineering.

We're all a bit sick of the gloom and doom about the jobs AI will destroy. Here’s one it will create in every company.

Jiaona Zhang, Chief Product Officer of  Laurel, recently said that the “AI workflows” role is one that will grow increasingly in demand. Totally agree. 

Most companies today are sprinkling AI co‑pilots on top of legacy processes and wondering why the P&L never budges. What's needed is a rework of the processes themselves. 

AI Ops focuses on rebuilding internal workflows to improve customer success and grow revenue. Think systematically deciding what’s automated and what’s AI‑assisted (emphasis on "systematically"). 

Zhang says this is massive opportunity for new grads. They are often more comfortable experimenting with AI tools and iterate faster than many mid‑career operators. 

Agreed but I would add a bit more nuance: AI fluency on its own is not enough. To redesign a sales, support, or ops process, you need domain understanding – the edge cases, incentives, KPIs, and “messy reality” of the function. 

That's where experience matters and middle and senior managers come in.

The way to make AI Ops really work is to pair AI‑native grads tightly with domain experts. Grads learn the business as they automate it, and managers learn how to augment processes with AI. 

I don’t buy into the ageism around AI adoption. I subscribe to the belief that people get comfortable as they are exposed to how things work. Such a pairing will help both the new grads and the managers level up. 

Plus, companies can then finally move past the AI pilot purgatory most are stuck in.
